13006-representative-plays-by-american-d:
Steele MacKay's Paul Kauvar; or, Anarchy anchors this volume of American drama from 1856 to 1911. The editor frames the play by its sociological purpose, not just its plot, and sets MacKay's old melodrama form against the realism of Galsworthy. Daly and Boucicault long held the American stage in their grip, while Howard, Belasco, and Herne began to break free.

Inside, large scenes and moving crowds give the play its force. Paul pledges silence under pressure, and Diane chooses her father's side over her own safety while Kauvar offers her shelter. The volume thus shows a theatre in change, from broad stage effects toward a harder, more modern kind of truth.
14876-the-forest-runners-a-story-of-the-:
Joseph A. Altsheler's story of the great war trail in early Kentucky follows forest runners through river, lone cabin, siege, flight and battle on the hill. Paul opens the tale, and what happened in the dark, a river bank, a change of places and an island in the lake follow.

A sudden meeting, belt bearers, Braxton Wyatt's ordeal, winter quarters and work and play widen the frontier picture. Altsheler, author of The Young Trailers, writes for boys who love woodcraft, tracking and danger. The forest runners are scouts and messengers in a border war, and their skill with trail, river and rifle carries the story from first alarm to last stand.
18154-calumet-k:
Merwin-Webster's 1904 novel takes its name from a huge grain elevator, Calumet K, meant to hold two million bushels. The contract went to MacBride and Company of Minneapolis in January, but work lagged, and by late October the great bins still stood unfinished. Ill luck had dogged Peterson, the constructor, since August.

MacBride then sends Charlie Bannon from a job at Duluth to take charge at Chicago. Bannon finds naked cribbing rising over shanties and lumber piles, with plank sidewalks raised above seas of mud. The novel follows the push to finish the elevator against time, weather, and bad luck. It is a work-site story about bosses, builders, and a building that must rise or fail.
25112-the-life-of-king-edward-vii-with-a:
J. Castell Hopkins's Life of King Edward VII, published in 1910 with many illustrations, follows the king from birth in 1841 through his long years as Prince of Wales. It ends with his accession in 1901 and death in May 1910. A closing sketch carries the story on to his son, King George V.

Chapters trace Edward's education, his tours of British America, the United States, the East, and India, his marriage and home life, his sporting tastes, and his work as an empire statesman. Hopkins writes as an admiring chronicler, and the book stands as a contemporary memorial volume, issued in the year of the king's death.
30431-calumet-k:
Merwin-Webster, authors of The Short Line War, tell a construction novel about Calumet K, a two million bushel grain elevator let to MacBride and Company of Minneapolis in January. Copyrighted in 1901 and published that October, the book follows a superstructure begun late in May and still far from complete at the end of October.

Ill luck dogs Peterson, the constructor, especially since August, and MacBride, head of the firm, dislikes unlucky men. After three months, patience wears thin and pressure mounts. The novel turns on contracts, deadlines, bad luck, and management, giving readers an industrial story of grain, steel, and human strain.
31050-a-new-order-of-fishlike-amphibia-f:
Theodore H. Eaton, Jr., and Peggy Lou Stewart wrote this paper on a new order of fishlike amphibia from the Pennsylvanian of Kansas. It was published in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume 12, number 4, pages 217 to 240, with twelve figures, on May 2, 1960. The quarry, locality KAN 1/D, lies about six miles northwest of Garnett in Anderson County, Kansas.

It sits two hundred yards southwest of the place where Petrolacosaurus kansensis was obtained. The Rock Lake shale is a thin member of the Stanton limestone formation, deposited under alternately marine and freshwater lagoon conditions. Peabody in 1958 had placed Hesperoherpeton in the order Anthracosauria, suborder Embolomeri, family Cricotidae. Study of a second, more complete specimen reveals more. It is a substantial fossil paper, rich in figures.
33361-ozma-of-oz-a-record-of-her-adventu:
L. Frank Baum's Ozma of Oz faithfully records the adventures of Ozma with Dorothy Gale of Kansas, the Yellow Hen, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, Tiktok, the Cowardly Lion, and the Hungry Tiger. Illustrated by John R. Neill, the book follows Dorothy on a new journey to Oz, where she meets old friends and new wonders, and where Ozma herself takes center stage.

Baum writes with his usual warmth and invention, blending humor, peril, and kindness in a tale for young readers. The book's charm lies in its odd, lovable characters and its bright, fairytale logic. For fans of the Wizard of Oz, Ozma of Oz is a delightful return to a beloved land, full of surprises for readers of every age.
33712-the-life-of-yakoob-beg-athalik-gha:
Demetrius Charles Boulger, a member of the Royal Asiatic Society, tells the life of Yakoob Beg, Athalik Ghazi and Badaulet, Ameer of Kashgar, in this 1878 London volume with map and appendix. Boulger writes with a twofold intention. The aim is to trace a soldier of fortune who rose without family standing, power, or even great genius to build an independent rule in Central Asia. He held it against many adversaries for twelve years. It is also to correct popular exaggeration of his hero.

Readers expecting Yakoob Beg lauded to the skies will be disappointed, Boulger warns: his subject was able and courageous, but his task in Kashgaria must be judged soberly. Dedicated to the author's father, Brian Austen Boulger, the book offers a Victorian biography of a Central Asian ruler at the height of the Great Game. It remains a detailed, if period-bound, source on Kashgar's brief independence.
486-ozma-of-oz-a-record-of-her-adventure:
L. Frank Baum brings Dorothy back to Oz in this tale, after a storm casts her ashore in the land of Ev. With Billina the yellow hen, Tik-Tok the machine man, and old friends, she faces Princess Langwidere's many heads and the Nome King, who holds Ev's royal family as ornaments. Eleven guesses decide their fate.

Baum writes with wit and warmth, letting Billina's sharp tongue save the day. The Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, and Cowardly Lion join the rescue. The book charms as a bright sequel, where courage, craft, and a hen's nerve beat a king's greed.
8153-the-young-engineers-in-arizona-or-l:
H. Irving Handcock wrote this adventure for boys about young engineers laying tracks across the man-killer quicksand in Arizona. The first chapter opens in Abe Morris's barber shop, where two customers, tucked up in white to the chin for haircuts, wager on which fly will leave its mirror first. From that comic start, the story moves to surveying, grading, and the dangers of desert engineering.

The novel follows the series formula: plucky young heroes, technical problems solved by brains and courage, and villains to outwit. Its Arizona setting gives it colour, from desert heat to treacherous ground. For young readers and collectors of boys' adventure series, it is a brisk tale of work and daring on the railroad frontier.
9931-k:
Mary Roberts Rinehart's novel opens on an old street of ancient houses, where a wandering man under thirty rents a little house. The street looks shabby but comfortable, like a well-worn coat, and the man hopes for peace: long evenings to read and quiet nights to sleep and forget.

No one at the little house asks much about references, and the man keeps his past to himself. Rinehart, queen of the American mystery romance, slowly reveals why he came and what follows him. Readers get suspense wrapped in domestic detail, as a new home becomes a place of secrets.
calumet-k:
Samuel Merwin, with Webster, wrote a novel of grain trade work, dated 1904. Its name is an elevator: Calumet K, a two million bushel house let to MacBride and Company of Minneapolis. Building work on the frame began late in May. End of October found it still far from done.

Ill luck dogged Peterson, the man on the job, most of all since August. MacBride had no love for luckless men. Three months' grit wore out, and a wire called Charlie Bannon south from Duluth. Home office orders sent Bannon to Chicago to take Peterson's place. Ten on a Monday found him at a trolley pane, eye on the bare bins past the shacks. Work pace, crew trust, and a boss's faith form the stakes the first pages lay out.
doe-osti-3016989-experiences-with-sycl-o:
Daniel Arndt, Damien Lebrun-Grandie, and Christian Trott of Oak Ridge National Laboratory wrote report ORNL/TM-2025/4398 in December 2025. It reports their experience running Kokkos on AMD graphics processors through the SYCL programming model. Kokkos is a performance portability library: write code once, then run it on chips from different makers. Hardware variety in supercomputing makes that portability valuable.

Kokkos supports backends for OpenMP, CUDA, HIP, and SYCL, so users can pick each vendor's preferred toolchain. The report focuses on the SYCL backend used with AMD hardware. One finding concerns reductions, the summing steps common in scientific code: the local memory variant beat the shuffle variant on Intel graphics processors, so the backend uses local memory by default. The authors also flag where that default runs into trouble on AMD. Porting teams get hard-won notes instead of marketing claims.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WinterKillsByRi: nsia-WinterKillsByRichardCondon Winter Kills By Richard Condon: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-slavic-aryan-vedas-a: Aleksandr Khinevich's Slavic-Aryan Vedas presents texts such as the Santiya Veda of Perun and the Haratya as ancient Slavic scripture. Mainstream scholars do not accept these works as old sources. The library holds the volume as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe material. It serves the study of modern mythmaking: new scriptures written for movements that want a very old past.
ozma-of-oz-a-record-of-her-adventures-wi:
L. Frank Baum's Ozma of Oz is the third Oz book. It records Princess Ozma's adventures with Dorothy Gale of Kansas. The long title delights in listing the company. The Yellow Hen, the Scarecrow, and the Tin Woodman come. Tiktok, the Cowardly Lion, and the Hungry Tiger follow. The contents run from The Girl in the Chicken Coop through the heads of Langwidere and the Nome King to Dorothy's magic belt.

In his author's note Baum credits the children. Their letters plead to know more about Dorothy, ask what became of the Cowardly Lion and what Ozma did after becoming ruler of Oz, and even suggest plots. This volume answers them, taking Dorothy by storm and shipwreck out of Kansas and into the land of Ev.
podcast-joerogan-jNOQadUbo-k:
Comedian James McCann joins Joe Rogan for episode 2488. McCann is an Australian comic who built a name with sharp, odd sets. Rogan's stage has become a rite for rising comics.

The v1 note for the episode stays spare, so the guest carries the hour. McCann trades stories of clubs, hecklers, and the road. Rogan tests his takes on America and its habits. The talk flows as a classic Rogan hang: long, loose, and funny. New listeners meet a fresh voice on the biggest platform comedy has. A spare record leaves his act to speak.
podcast-joerogan-xz7jtzGsa-k:
Researcher Jacques Vallee and filmmaker James Fox join Joe Rogan together in episode 1574 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Fox directed The Phenomenon and other well-known UFO films. Vallee brings decades of case research, giving the pair a scientist-and-storyteller balance.

Fox shares what he learned filming witnesses, officials, and crash-site claims around the world. Vallee adds the patterns he sees across thousands of reports and warns against easy answers. Rogan guides them through famous cases old and new. Serious listeners get two of the field's best-known voices in one long conversation.
podcast-joerogan-yWrfEclkC_k:
America's opioid crisis, and the drug industry's share of blame, is the subject of this Joe Rogan Experience segment. Millions became addicted after pain pills were sold as safe and pushed hard by makers and marketers. Rogan and his guest tell the story plain, as an American tragedy.

They trace how aggressive sales, friendly doctors, and weak oversight flooded towns with pills. The talk covers the human cost in overdoses and broken families that followed. Questions of profit and punishment run through the whole account. For the grieving and the angry alike, it lays out how the pills, the profits, and the bodies connect.
representative-plays-by-american-dramati:
Paul Kauvar; or, Anarchy represents Steele Mackaye in this set of American plays, with an essay weighing his place in the theatre. Mackaye lived from 1844 to 1894. The essay grants his play a serious social purpose, yet finds the old romantic form too weak to carry such matter well.

Mackaye's strength lay in vigour: large scenes, mob movement, and a big brush, as critic Nym Crinkle put it. He built a double stage for the little Madison Square playhouse, a first step toward later stage machines. Trained under Delsarte, he preached natural acting, and once held Longfellow, Bryant, and Edwin Booth spellbound for two hours at the Lotos Club.
the-forest-runners-a-story-of-the-great-:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Forest Runners as a tale of the great war trail in early Kentucky, first printed in 1908. It stands in his Young Trailers series with The Young Trailers and The Keepers of the Trail.

The front pages list Altsheler's many sets: French and Indian War tales, Texan tales, Civil War tales, and Great West tales. His boys' books mix scouting, hunting, and war paths with close woodcraft. In this tale young runners cross a Kentucky thick with foes, where a dropped sign or a snapped twig can cost a life, and speed and silence are a boy's best arms.
the-young-engineers-in-arizona-or-laying:
H. Irving Hancock opens The Young Engineers in Arizona in Abe Morris's barber shop. Two customers bet on flies sitting on their mirrors. The wager jumps from ten dollars to twenty. Each man sits tucked in white, mid-haircut, watching his fly. The bet's maker is Jim Duff, a notorious local gambler. Hancock calls him among the meanest Arizona ever hosted.

Traditions about honest gamblers, the narrator scoffs, fool only newcomers. Tom Reade and Harry Hazelton, the young engineers, will face such men. Their job lays railroad tracks across dangerous quicksand. The subtitle calls it the man-killer quicksand. Boys' adventure readers get gambling, grit, and engineering hazards combined.
